summary: This informational memo specifies the S-expression data structure representation created for SPKI certificates (RFC 2692), meant to be more widely usable. It has been used elsewhere and has implementations in many languages.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a simple way of writing nested lists of data so computers can read it. It was invented for digital certificates but works for other things too.

subtitle: A simple notation for encoding nested data structures

tldr.problem: Digital certificates and cryptographic systems need a way to represent and transport complex, hierarchical data (like lists of keys, policies, and credentials) that is readable, compact, transportable over unreliable channels, and supports canonical forms for signing.
tldr.mechanism: S-expressions use parentheses and simple representations—quoted strings, hexadecimal values, and base-64 encoding—to express octet-strings and nested lists of data. The format is flexible enough for human reading and compact enough for machine parsing.
tldr.outcome: S-expressions have become a widely used notation for certificates, configurations, and protocol messages. They are simpler than XML and more readable than ASN.1 DER, and the format has implementations in Python, Ruby, C, and other languages.

facts.label: Primary design goal
facts.value: Represent arbitrary data for SPKI certificates

facts.label: Canonical form marker
facts.value: Verbatim strings with no whitespace in lists

facts.label: Character set
facts.value: ASCII for most forms; verbatim and quoted strings allow any octet

today: RFC 9804 is an Informational RFC and a modernized version of a 1997 draft that was never formally submitted to the IETF. S-expressions remain in active use in cryptographic libraries (libgcrypt, GnuPG, RNP) and are referenced in modern standards. The format is stable and has proven interoperability across multiple implementations and programming languages. It serves as an alternative to XML, JSON, and ASN.1 for applications where both machine efficiency and human readability matter.

sections.title: The Data Representation Problem
sections.content:
Cryptographic systems like SPKI certificates, OpenPGP keys, and secure configurations need to store and transmit structured data: public keys, identities, policies, time bounds, and so on. The data is often hierarchical—a certificate might contain a list of policies, each of which is itself a list of rules.

The designer needs a format that meets several goals: it must be readable by humans (so administrators can inspect and debug), compact for storage and transmission, robust to transport over channels that might corrupt or filter certain byte values (like email or some network links), and unambiguous when used for digital signatures (where changing even one bit should invalidate the signature).

In the 1990s, ASN.1 with Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) was the cryptographic standard, but it was complex and hard for non-experts to parse. S-expressions, inspired by the LISP programming language, offer a simpler, more flexible alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a way to write a certificate or a secret key so that computers can read it, people can understand it, and you can sign it with a digital signature. It should work even over email or unreliable networks.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
An S-expression is either a simple string (a sequence of octets) or a list of S-expressions. That is all. The entire format is defined recursively from these two building blocks.

A simple string can be written in multiple ways:

  • Token form: Just write the text as-is, like subject or not-before. A token must not start with a digit and can only contain letters, numbers, and punctuation marks.
  • Quoted string form: Write text in double quotes with C-style escape sequences, like hello followed by a newline.
  • Verbatim form (length-prefixed): Write the length in decimal, a colon, and the exact bytes. This works for binary data and strings with special characters.
  • Hexadecimal form: Encode bytes as hex between hash marks, like #48656C6C6F# representing hello.
  • Base-64 form: Encode bytes using base-64 between vertical bars, like |aGVsbG8=| representing hello.

Lists are written with parentheses containing a list of three elements: the token subject, the token alice, and a sub-list containing role and admin.
sections.plainLanguage: You write a list with parentheses like (name Alice age 30). Each piece of data can be a word, quoted text, numbers in different formats, or another nested list.

sections.title: Three Representation Forms
sections.content:
S-expressions support three different concrete representations, each suited to a different purpose:

Canonical representation is deterministic and unambiguous. It encodes every string in verbatim form (length-prefixed) and lists with no extra whitespace. This is used for digital signatures: when signing an S-expression, both parties must produce the identical canonical bytes, bit-for-bit, so the signature is stable and verifiable.

Basic transport representation is either canonical or the canonical form wrapped in base-64 inside braces, like {aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=}. This is for transmission over channels that might corrupt binary data. A receiver can decode it back to the original S-expression.

Advanced (display) representation is flexible and human-friendly. It allows all the string formats (quoted, hex, base-64, tokens), optional lengths, whitespace for readability, and even display hints (metadata about how to render an octet-string, like [image/gif] or [text/plain; charset=utf-8]). This is for documentation, debugging, and configuration files.
sections.plainLanguage: The canonical form is strict and unambiguous—good for signatures. Basic transport wraps it in base-64 for email and unreliable channels. Advanced form is flexible and readable for people and configuration files.

sections.title: In Practice: SPKI Certificates and Beyond
sections.content:
S-expressions originated in the SPKI project for certificates, but have found use in other systems. The libgcrypt library (part of GnuPG) uses S-expressions internally and in file formats. Ribose's RNP cryptographic library uses them for configuration and key storage. Even modern standards like XML-Signature reference S-expressions as an inspiration.

An example SPKI certificate might look like:

  (certificate
    (issuer "example.com")
    (subject alice@example.com)
    (public-key 65537 12345... ) 
    (valid (not-before 2023-01-01) (not-after 2025-01-01))
  )

The structure is clear: a certificate is a list of fields. Parsing is straightforward—no state machines or backtracking required. Signing just means hashing the canonical form. Extending the format (adding new fields) is easy: the parser can ignore unknown fields without breaking.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate written in S-expressions is a list of pieces of information. It is easy to read, easy to parse, easy to sign, and easy to extend with new fields.

sections.title: Design Goals and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC lists the design goals for S-expressions:

  • Generality: represent any data, from text to binary to nested structures.
  • Readability: someone can look at it and understand the structure without a specification.
  • Economy: compact representation; canonical form is compact.
  • Transportability: work over email, FTP, and channels that filter certain byte values.
  • Flexibility: easy to modify and extend; missing fields do not break parsing.
  • Canonicalization: produce a unique, deterministic form for signatures.
  • Efficiency: allow in-memory representations that are fast to process.

In trade-offs, S-expressions prioritize simplicity and human readability over perfect compactness (JSON and CBOR are more compact for certain data). They are less standardized than XML or ASN.1, but simpler to implement correctly. For applications that need both machine and human understanding—like cryptographic credentials, configuration management, and protocol messages—the trade-off favors S-expressions.
sections.plainLanguage: S-expressions are designed to be readable by people, compact, work on any kind of network, easy to extend, and able to be signed unambiguously.

data.title: Four ways to represent the string hello
data.code:
hello                    ; token form
"hello"                  ; quoted string form
5:hello                  ; verbatim (length-prefixed) form
#68656C6C6F#             ; hexadecimal form
|aGVsbG8=|               ; base-64 form
